creating duplicates, so a re-entry after a partial failure or a
retried job continues from where it left off instead of standing up
a second copy of the stack. The same property is what makes the
post-install steps and the OIDC wiring safe to reach more than once.

## A note on capacity

Before a composed install starts, Flui sums the resource requests of
every component that will be included and checks them against what
the cluster has free, refusing the install if there is not enough
room (a safety margin is kept). This is the same capacity gate that
guards any install; the exact CPU-vs-memory accounting is covered in
[The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/).

## Where to read next

- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/) — the
  shared envelope, including the composed-manifest surface.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/) —
  the three flavours of catalog entry and where composed sits.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — what each
  component becomes once it is running, and the capacity gate in
  full.
- [`flui deploy`](/cli/deploy/) — the command-level reference for
  installing and deploying.

sections.title: Inference and BYO LLM
sections.body:
Flui has features that need a large language model: the assistant
that drives the platform in natural language, and the AI assist in
the database console. Those features should not care *where* the
model comes from. So Flui draws a clean line: anything that wants
inference asks for a single, normalized endpoint, and a resolver
behind that line works out how to produce it.

That endpoint is always the same shape — an OpenAI-compatible
`{ baseUrl, apiKey }`. No Flui abstraction sits over the model
itself; the model ids, the request format, the streaming are all
plain OpenAI-compatible. The only thing Flui owns is *how the
endpoint is sourced and credentialed*, and that is where the two
ways below differ.

## Two ways to get an endpoint

There are exactly two sources of inference, and they are
deliberately different things.

### Native — inference as a provider capability

Some cloud providers also run an OpenAI-compatible inference
service. When they do, Flui models that as a capability the
provider declares, just like firewalls or DNS — an
`InferenceCapability` carrying a `baseUrl`, an optional curated
`models` list for display, a `euDataResidency` flag, and a
`sharesComputeCredentials` flag.

The interesting flag is `sharesComputeCredentials`. For Scaleway it
is `true`: the provider's inference service authenticates with the
**same IAM secret** Flui already holds to provision your
infrastructure. So when you point Flui at a Scaleway account, you
get inference for free — there is no separate AI key to create,
paste or rotate. Flui reuses the existing compute credential as the
inference bearer token.

A provider that *only* did inference — that you would never use for
compute — would not have a compute credential to borrow. For that
case Flui supports a dedicated credential whose purpose is
inference rather than compute, kept under the same credential model
as everything else. Scaleway just doesn't need one, because its one
credential already covers both.

The curated `models` list on the capability is only a placeholder
for display before a key exists. Once Flui has a working
credential, the **live** model list is read straight from
`{baseUrl}/models` — so the models you can pick are always the ones
the provider actually offers right now, not a list baked into Flui.

### BYO connection — bring your own endpoint

The second source is a connection *you* configure: any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint — OpenAI, Mistral, a Claude-compatible
gateway, or a server you run yourself. This is **not** a provider.
It declares no capabilities and provisions no infrastructure. It is
pure connection config: a `base_url`, an API key (stored
encrypted), an optional list of `models`, and an `is_default`
flag.

These live behind their own small API under `inference/connections`
— you can list them, create one, validate it against its endpoint,
and delete it. Validation actually calls the endpoint, so a bad
key or wrong URL is caught when you save it, not the first time the
assistant tries to answer a question.

The split matters: native inference is something a provider *has*,
and you get it by virtue of connecting that provider; a BYO
connection is something *you bring*, independent of any provider,
and it works the same whether or not you run any Flui-managed
infrastructure at all.

## How the default endpoint is chosen

Most of the time the assistant doesn't name a specific source — it
just asks for "the" inference endpoint. The resolver answers that
with a fixed preference order:

1. **A configured native provider**, EU-first by the order
   providers are declared. If an inference-capable provider has a
   usable credential, that wins.
2. Otherwise, **the BYO connection flagged as default**.
3. Otherwise, **any single configured connection** — when there is
   exactly one, it is implicitly the default, so the resolver uses
   it rather than failing for lack of an explicit flag.

If none of those produce an endpoint, resolution fails cleanly with
"no inference endpoint configured" rather than guessing. The
ordering favours native providers first because, when one is
present, it usually means inference is already paid for and
credentialed through the same account you provision with — the
lowest-friction path.

## EU data residency is first-class

`euDataResidency` is a property of the capability, surfaced
alongside each native provider, not a footnote. For a self-hosted
platform that may be running under European data rules, *where the
prompt goes* is part of the decision, so Flui makes it visible at
the point you choose a provider — Scaleway's inference, for
example, declares EU residency. BYO connections point wherever you
configure them, so residency there is your call by construction.

## Recommended models

Picking a model id from a raw `/models` list is not obvious — names
are version-pinned and not portable across providers, and some are
a bad fit for tool use or cost more than you'd want for a first
run. Flui ships an opinionated, **overridable** recommendation
policy to smooth that.

The policy is a config file at
`assistant/config/recommended-models.json`. It names a
`recommendedProvider` to get started with — currently **Mistral**,
with the model `mistral-small-2506`, called out for its generous
free tier — and then, per provider, a curated list of
version-pinned model ids with short descriptions. Some entries
carry a caveat `note` (for instance, a stronger model marked "not
recommended on free plan") so the trade-off is visible before you
switch. The whole file can be replaced via an environment override,
so an operator can re-point the recommendations without a code
change.

These recommendations are read at startup, validated, and exposed
through the assistant API so the dashboard can preselect a sensible
default instead of dropping you into an unfiltered model list.

## Who consumes inference

The resolved endpoint is the single seam every AI feature sits on:

- **The Flui Assistant** — the natural-language layer over the
  platform — runs against whatever the resolver returns. See
  [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/).
- **The database console's AI assist** — the helper that turns a
  question into a query — uses the same resolved endpoint. See
  [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/).

Because both go through one resolver, configuring inference once —
native or BYO — lights up every AI feature at the same time, with
the same data-residency and credential story.

## Where to read next

- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/)
  — why inference is modelled as a provider capability, like
  firewalls or DNS, rather than a special case.
- [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/)
  — the primary consumer of the resolved endpoint.
- [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/) —
  the other consumer, where AI assist turns questions into queries.

sections.title: The Flui Assistant and MCP
sections.body:
Most platforms bolt a chatbot on at the end and hope it doesn't
say anything embarrassing. Flui treats its assistant as a real
surface of the product, with the same care the rest of the
platform gets: it answers from a compiled knowledge base rather
than free-associating, it can actually *do* things through a
shared tool registry, and every action it can take is governed by
the same scope model whether a human is driving it in the
dashboard or an external agent is calling it over MCP.

This chapter is about the shape of that choice and — more
importantly — the safety model underneath it, because the
load-bearing part of an assistant that can deploy and uninstall
your apps is *what stops it doing the wrong one*.

## Two surfaces, one tool registry

There are two ways into the same capabilities:

- **The in-product assistant** — the chat surface inside Flui's
  dashboard. You ask a question or a request in natural language;
  it answers from the docs, and when you ask it to *act* it runs
  an agentic tool-use loop on your behalf.
- **The MCP server** — a [Model Context
  Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) endpoint that
  exposes the *same* tools to external agents (your own scripts,
  an IDE agent, another LLM application).

The point of sharing is that a tool is written once. The same
registry (`ALL_TOOLS` in the code) backs both the in-process
assistant loop and the MCP server, so there is no second,
divergent surface to keep in sync — and, crucially, no second
place where the safety checks could drift apart. Both go through
the same scope tiers and the same destructive gate, described
below.

Both surfaces get their LLM from Flui's inference layer rather
than holding a hard-coded provider — see
[Inference and bring-your-own-LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/)
for how that endpoint is resolved.

## The assistant answers from a knowledge base, not from memory

The assistant does not reach into a general-purpose model's
training data to answer questions about Flui. Instead, Flui's
documentation is compiled into a **knowledge base** — a single
versioned artifact (`kb.json`) built by a script from the
concept docs, the CLI prose, a generated CLI reference, the
`flui.yaml` schema, and a hand-authored *guardrails* file. The
assistant answers strictly from this corpus.

This grounding is a deliberate choice to keep answers tied to the
facts. The guardrails make the contract explicit: the assistant's
knowledge *is* exactly the corpus it is handed — it is asked not to
invent commands, flags, manifest fields, or version numbers, and if
the answer isn't in the corpus it says so and points you at `flui
<command> --help` or the docs rather than guessing. The intent is
to keep the assistant inside what it actually knows and to minimise
the chance of an answer drifting from the documentation — not to
assume it would otherwise be wrong. The knowledge base is also
stamped with the CLI/platform/schema versions it was built against,
so the assistant can tell you which version it is reasoning about.

**This is why keeping these docs accurate matters.** The page you
are reading is one of the sources that gets compiled into that
knowledge base. An inaccurate doc is not just wrong on the website
— it becomes a wrong answer the assistant gives with confidence.

### A scope gate that also routes

Sending the whole corpus to the model on every message would be
slow and expensive (it is a large prefill). Flui avoids that with
a single cheap LLM call — a *guard* step — that does two jobs at
once:

1. **Scope gate.** It decides whether your message is on-topic for
   Flui at all. A genuinely off-topic question (the weather,
   philosophy, general trivia) is refused with a short, warm
   message *in your own language* that says the assistant only
   helps with Flui — it does not answer the off-topic question.
   The bias is strongly toward answering: greetings, follow-ups,
   and anything that plausibly concerns running apps on Flui are
   treated as on-topic.
2. **Router.** For an on-topic message, the same call returns the
   ids of the one-to-four most relevant knowledge sections. Only
   those sections are injected into the answering prompt, keeping
   it small.

So one inexpensive model call refuses the irrelevant and
narrows the relevant — before the more expensive answering call
ever runs.

### The agentic tool-use loop

When you ask the assistant to *do* something, it runs an agentic
loop: the model can call tools, see their results, and call more
tools, up to a bounded number of iterations, before it writes a
final answer. In the dashboard this is streamed over Server-Sent
Events, so you watch the text and the individual tool steps appear
live rather than waiting for a wall of output.

The loop is built defensively, so it stays reliable even on
medium-to-small models rather than depending on a large one. A few
of those safeguards:

- **A URL guard.** Application endpoint URLs are passed through
  only when they actually came from a tool result; anything else is
  stripped before it reaches you. So a link you get is one the
  platform produced, not one assembled in the answer.
- **Doc-link surfacing.** The sections the router grounded the
  answer in are turned, deterministically, into links to the
  published docs — the documentation URLs are produced by Flui, not
  composed in the prompt.
- **Parameter recovery and rate-limit handling.** If a tool call
  comes back malformed, or a provider's per-minute limit is hit,
  the loop recovers and retries rather than failing the whole turn.

Taken together, these are also why the assistant does not need a
large frontier model. The corpus handed to it is already narrowed
by the router, the answers are grounded in that corpus, and the
guards above are deterministic rather than left to the model — so a
**medium-to-small model is enough**, which is exactly what Flui's
inference layer recommends by default. See
[Inference and bring-your-own-LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/).

The tools span app lifecycle, deploy, debugging, the catalog,
infrastructure, and GitHub-repo onboarding — the same operations
you would otherwise reach for in the CLI or dashboard.

## The safety model

Everything above is convenience. This section is the contract.

### Scopes, ordered into tiers

Every tool declares a scope, and scopes are ordered into four
**tiers** by blast radius:

```
read  →  plan  →  write  →  destructive
```

- **read** — list and inspect: applications, the catalog,
  observability/logs.
- **plan** — non-mutating analysis, e.g. validating a `flui.yaml`
  spec.
- **write** — state-changing operations: install, deploy, scale,
  restart, stop, connect a repo.
- **destructive** — delete and uninstall.

A grant at a tier implies every lower tier, so granting *write*
also grants *read* and *plan*.

### Default-deny

The system is **default-deny**. A tool runs only if its scope is
in the calling principal's granted set. An authenticated principal
with *no explicit grant* gets the safe default — **read and plan
only**. To get *write* or *destructive*, the scope has to be
granted deliberately (on an API key or as an identity-provider
role), and an explicit least-privilege grant always wins: a scoped
API key stays least-privilege even for an admin.

The MCP tool groups map onto these tiers: **application**,
**catalog**, **observability**, **spec**, **infrastructure**, and
**repo**.

### The destructive gate (the load-bearing rule)

Deleting and uninstalling are special. A destructive tool requires
**both** of these to be true before it can run:

1. The principal holds a **destructive scope**, *and*
2. A **server-wide environment flag**, `MCP_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE`,
   is set to `true`.

The flag is **off by default**. When it is off, a destructive
operation is refused *deterministically* — never offered, never
retried — with an "an administrator must enable them" style
message. This is not the model choosing to behave; it is code
refusing before the tool body ever runs, and the refusal is
audited.

The same gate exists on both surfaces, but the *human* checkpoint
differs by context:

- **In the interactive assistant**, a write or destructive action
  pauses for **explicit human confirmation** — the action comes
  back as a pending step you approve before anything changes. (And
  if a destructive op is disabled by the flag, the assistant
  doesn't even offer the confirmation — it can't honour it, so it
  tells you how to enable it instead.)
- **In headless MCP**, there is no human in the loop to confirm,
  so the **environment flag is the checkpoint**. An operator
  decides, once, at the server level, whether external agents are
  allowed to perform destructive operations at all.

There is one more guard worth naming: the loop is **idempotent**
across a conversation. A write or destructive action that already
succeeded won't run a second time if it is re-proposed — so an
"install" or a "delete" can't fire twice from a repeated
suggestion.

### Why this shape

The thinking is blast-radius first. The most useful thing an
assistant can do is also the most dangerous, so rather than rely on
every proposal being correct, the design makes a wrong one cheap
and recoverable instead of catastrophic — defence in depth, not a
verdict on the model. Read and plan are free to flow because they
change nothing. Writes need a human's yes (or a deliberate scope).
And the irreversible operations — delete, uninstall — need an
operator to have turned them on *at the server* in addition to
everything else. The goal is that no single mistaken token, and no
single off turn, can quietly destroy your data.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Inference and bring-your-own-LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/) —
  how the assistant and MCP get their LLM endpoint, and how to
  point them at your own model.
- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/) — where the
  authenticated principals (and the scoped machine-to-machine keys
  the MCP surface authenticates) come from.
- [Observability is not an afterthought](/concepts/08-observability-as-first-class/) —
  the logs and metrics the assistant's read tools surface when you
  ask it to debug an app.

sections.title: The database console
sections.body:
When you run a database on Flui — a Postgres or MariaDB picked from
the catalog, a Redis or Valkey cache bundled with an app — you
eventually need to look inside it: run a query, check a row, see
what keys are taking up space. Historically that meant either
exposing the database to the internet (a bad idea), bolting on a
separate web tool like pgweb (one more thing to host and secure),
or reaching for a native client and a hand-rolled tunnel.

The database console removes that gap. It is a first-party SQL and
key-value runner built into the dashboard and served through Flui's
own backend — no extra tool to install, and no public database
endpoint anywhere. This chapter is the conceptual picture: which
engines it speaks, how it connects, what it deliberately will *not*
do, and where the natural-language helper draws its safety line.

## What it covers today

The console is organised around two engine *families*, each with
its own surface:

- **SQL** — Postgres and MariaDB. A query editor that runs SQL,
  a schema browser that introspects tables, columns, primary keys
  and foreign keys, and a connection-info panel.
- **Key-value** — Redis and Valkey. A keyspace overview (counts,
  not contents), a key scan, a value reader, and a command runner.

These map directly to the building blocks Flui already ships in its
catalog. The engine is not something you configure — Flui detects
it from the database's container image, and falls back to detecting
a SQL engine from the user/database environment variables it has
set. Adding a new engine is a matter of one engine profile plus one
adapter on Flui's side; the query, transport and helper layers stay
engine-agnostic.

## Read-only by default, and it means it

The single most important property of the SQL console is that every
query runs **read-only by default**. This is not a UI checkbox that
filters out the word `DELETE` — it is enforced at the database
session itself. For Postgres, each query opens a transaction, sets
it `READ ONLY`, applies the limits, and then **rolls back** rather
than commits. A statement that tries to write fails at the engine;
nothing it did persists, because the transaction is discarded
regardless.

Two more guards ride along on every query:

- **A statement timeout of about 30 seconds.** A query that runs
  away — a missing `WHERE`, an accidental cross join — is cut off
  by the database rather than holding a connection open
  indefinitely.
- **A row cap of about 1000 rows.** The grid shows the first slice
  and tells you the result was truncated. The console is for
  inspection, not for bulk export.

The key-value side follows the same shape. Browsing — the keyspace
summary, the key scan, reading a value — is inherently read-only.
The command runner passes through a **read-only gate**: arbitrary
commands are allowed only when they are reads; a write or
destructive command (a `FLUSHALL`, say) is rejected unless the
write path is explicitly enabled.

The reason for all of this is blast radius. The console is the
everyday "let me just check something" tool, and the everyday tool
should be incapable of breaking the database it is inspecting. The
write path exists in the design, but it is gated, audited, and not
the default.

## How it connects: the owner-credential model

To run a query, the console has to authenticate to the database.
Today it does that with the building block's **own owner (superuser)
credentials** — the same username, password and database that the
catalog generated when it installed the building block.

Those credentials are not stored a second time and are not typed in
by you. Flui reads them, at the moment of the query, straight from
the Kubernetes Secret that the building block already owns (the
`<slug>-secret` the install generated). SQL engines carry a user
and a database; key-value caches authenticate with the password
alone, and are often deployed with no auth at all, in which case the
console connects anonymously. The engine-specific details — which
Secret key holds the password, which port to use, which environment
variables name the user and database — come from a per-engine
profile, so the connection logic itself never branches on the
engine name.

This is the honest description of the current state: **everyone who
can open the console connects as the database owner.** That is
acceptable today because the console's default is read-only and
every action is audited server-side — but it is a known limitation,
not a destination.

### The forward path: per-user roles

The piece of the design that makes the owner-credential model
temporary is a deliberate seam. The thing that turns "this app" into
"a live connection" is a single, narrow interface — a connection
*resolver*. The implementation in place resolves the building
block's owner Secret and reports the role as `owner`. A future
implementation will provision or resolve a **dedicated, per-Flui-user
role** on the database and report the role as `user` — and it will
slot in behind the exact same interface, with no change to the query
layer, the transport, or the helper above it. That is the path from
"everyone is the owner" to "each person connects as themselves, with
their own grants."

## How the dashboard reaches the database

Flui databases are **not exposed outside the cluster network.**
There is no public database endpoint to firewall, rotate, or worry
about. So how does a console running in your browser reach a
database sitting on a private cluster?

It goes **through Flui's backend.** For each query, the backend
opens a short-lived in-cluster tunnel to the database pod, runs the
query over it, and tears the tunnel down again when the call
returns. The browser never talks to the database directly; it talks
to the Flui API, which is the only thing that ever holds a
connection. Nothing about the database's address or password is
handed to the browser.

That same property is why the connection-info panel is safe to show.
It returns the coordinates you need to reason about a connection —
engine, database name, user, in-cluster port — and **never the
password.** The password does not travel over the HTTP API at all.

## Connecting a native client from your machine

The in-browser console is for inspection. When you want the real
thing — `psql`, the `mariadb` client, DBeaver, or an ORM pointed at
the database from your laptop — the CLI gives you two commands that
honour the same "no public endpoint" rule. They are covered in full
on the [databases CLI page](/cli/databases/); the shape is:

- **`flui db tunnel <app>`** opens a local tunnel to the database.
  It forwards through the control plane over SSH and an in-cluster
  port-forward, bound to `127.0.0.1` on your machine — so the
  database becomes reachable as `localhost:<port>` for the life of
  the command, and nothing is opened to the outside world. It then
  prints a ready-to-paste connection string and a client command.
- **`flui db credentials <app>`** prints the in-cluster address and
  credentials for connecting another app *running on Flui* to the
  database, plus a `DATABASE_URL`. The password is read from the
  in-cluster Secret over SSH and is hidden unless you pass `--show`.

In both cases the password is fetched straight from the cluster
Secret over SSH — never from the API — which is the same discipline
the in-browser console follows.

## The AI helper is data-blind

Both consoles offer a natural-language helper: describe what you
want in plain English, and it returns a SQL query (or a Redis
command) plus an explanation, which you then review and run yourself.
The helper never executes anything on your behalf — and, more
importantly, it never *sees your data*.

This is the load-bearing safety property, so it is worth being
precise. When you ask the SQL helper a question, what gets sent to
the language model is exactly three things:

1. **The schema** — table and column names, types, primary keys and
   foreign keys. Structure only.
2. **Your question** — the natural-language prompt.
3. **A curated, per-engine knowledge base** — Flui's own baked-in
   notes on the engine's dialect, query patterns and gotchas
   (a distinct corpus for Postgres, for MariaDB, and for
   Redis/Valkey), so the suggestions fit the engine you are actually
   running.

What is **never** sent is any row data. The helper introspects the
schema, but it does not read, sample, or forward the contents of a
single row. The key-value helper is even more conservative: it sees
only the keyspace *summary* — a key count and a per-type breakdown —
never key names or values. This "data-blind by contract" design is
what makes it safe to use a hosted model against a production
database: the model can reason about *shape* without ever being
exposed to the *contents*.

The query the helper writes still runs under all the same rules as a
hand-typed one — read-only by default, the statement timeout, the
row cap. A suggestion that would change data is flagged as a mutation
so the dashboard can put a confirmation in front of it, but the
read-only transaction underneath is the real boundary; the flag is
only a hint.

The helper does not ship its own model. It uses the same inference
layer the rest of Flui's assistant features use, which means it
inherits whatever you have configured there — Flui's native
inference or your own bring-your-own provider. That story has its
own chapter:
[Inference and bring-your-own LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/).

## What it is, and what it is not

To set expectations cleanly:

- It **is** a fast, safe way to inspect the databases you already
  run on Flui — query, browse schema, scan keys, get a query draft
  — without exposing them and without a second tool to host.
- It is **not** a full database administration suite, a migration
  runner, or a bulk-export tool. The row cap and the read-only
  default are deliberate; they are what make it the right tool to
  reach for first.

## Where to read next

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — databases are
  apps in Flui's model, with the same lifecycle, logs and metrics as
  anything else you run.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/) —
  where the Postgres, MariaDB, Redis and Valkey building blocks the
  console operates on come from.
- [Inference and bring-your-own LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/) —
  the inference layer the data-blind helper draws on.
- [The databases CLI](/cli/databases/) — `flui db tunnel` and
  `flui db credentials` for connecting native clients.

# Flui CLI reference (generated)

> Generated from `oclif manifest` for flui CLI `0.9.2`. Do not edit by hand —
> regenerate with `pnpm kb:cli-ref`. This is the assistant's ground truth for commands.

CLI version: **0.9.2** · commands: **188**

## (root)

### `flui deploy`

Deploy an application from a flui.yaml manifest to a cluster. Supports both kind:CatalogApp (pre-built image) and kind:Application (source build via GitHub Actions). Author a manifest with `flui app init <framework>`; see every field with `flui app manifest`.

Arguments:
  - `file` — Path to flui.yaml manifest (default: ./flui.yaml)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Target cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-r, --repo` — GitHub repository full name owner/repo (default: auto-detect from git remote origin). Required for kind:Application.
  - `-b, --branch` — Git branch to deploy (default: auto-detect current branch). Used for kind:Application.
  - `-d, --domain` — Custom FQDN for the app (default: auto-assign from cluster DNS zone)
  - `--name` — Display name override (default: metadata.name from manifest)
  - `-e, --env` — Environment variable override in KEY=VALUE format. Repeatable.
  - `--env-file` — Path to a KEY=VALUE file of env overrides (one per line, # comments and blank lines ignored). Values never appear in the process arguments, so this is the safe way to pass secrets. --env entries take precedence.
  - `--detach` — Return immediately after triggering the build/deploy without waiting for completion. Use `flui app status <name>` to track progress.
  - `--no-build` — Skip the GitHub Actions build and re-deploy the current image. Useful for fast iterations on flui.yaml config (env, ports, healthcheck, endpoint) without rebuilding. If the app was deleted, falls back to the GHCR latest tag for {owner}/{repoName}.
  - `--image` — Deploy a specific image reference (e.g. ghcr.io/owner/repo:sha). Skips the build pipeline. Useful for rollback to a known tag, or to deploy from GHCR when the app was deleted from Flui.
  - `--skip-endpoint` — Skip DNS and TLS provisioning (kind:CatalogApp only)
  - `--no-tls` — Provision the endpoint with DNS only, without a per-app TLS certificate (kind:CatalogApp). Overrides the manifest domain.tls. Avoids Let's Encrypt rate limits; the app is served over HTTP.
  - `--cert-challenge` [http-01 | dns-01] — ACME challenge for the app endpoint (kind:CatalogApp). http-01 works without a DNS zone and forces a per-host cert; dns-01 needs a cluster DNS zone with a wildcard issuer. Default: derived from cluster config.
  - `--cert-provider` [lets-encrypt | lets-encrypt-staging] — Certificate issuer for the app endpoint (kind:CatalogApp). Default: cluster default.
  - `--hostname` [ip | domain] — How the app is exposed (kind:CatalogApp): ip (nip.io) or domain (cluster DNS zone). Default: derived from manifest/cluster.
  - `--no-wait` — Alias for --detach (kind:CatalogApp compat)
  - `--validate-only` — Validate the manifest locally against the flui.cloud/v1beta1 schema without deploying (no cluster or login needed). Combine with --json for machine-readable output.
  - `--json` — With --validate-only, emit the result as JSON: { valid, kind, errors[], warnings[] }.
  - `--skip-checks` — Bypass the framework post-checks (e.g. Next.js standalone output). Only use when you are certain the Dockerfile will succeed despite the warnings.
  - `--allow-master` — Allow dedicated (node-local) storage to be placed on the control-plane node when the cluster has no worker. Escape hatch for single-node clusters (kind:CatalogApp).
  - `--api-url` — Override the API base URL (e.g. http://localhost:3000/api/v1) for local-API testing against an unreleased backend. Default: active profile.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> ./apps/api/flui.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --repo acme/my-app --branch main
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --detach
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --env DATABASE_URL=postgres://... --env API_KEY=secret
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --validate-only
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --cluster my-cluster
```

### `flui reconcile`

Reconcile CLI state with API (DNS configuration)

Flags:
  - `-t, --type` [dns | all] (default: ["all"]) — Reconciliation type(s) to execute (default: all)
  - `--api-url` — Flui API URL (default: from config or http://localhost:3000/api/v1)
  - `--dry-run` — Show what would be reconciled without making changes

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --type dns
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --dry-run
```

### `flui search-assist-test`

THROWAWAY: drive the search copilot (assist + optional run) via CLI auth, for validation.

Arguments:
  - `appId` (required) — OpenSearch application id

Flags:
  - `--prompt` — Single NL prompt (omit to use --suite)
  - `--index` — Active index for the prompt
  - `--suite` — Run the built-in 12-prompt suite
  - `--run` — Also execute the generated query via /search/query
  - `--exec-os` — Run the generated body directly against this OpenSearch URL (e.g. http://localhost:9201) — proves runnability without touching the cluster
  - `--api-url` — API base URL override (e.g. http://localhost:3000/api/v1)
  - `--raw` — Dev Tools raw call: "METHOD /path" (e.g. "GET /_cat/indices")
  - `--body` — JSON body for --raw
  - `--body-file` — Read the JSON body from a file (overrides --body)
  - `--allow-writes` — Send readOnly:false with --raw/--assist-raw (lets mutations run)
  - `--assist-raw` — Use the Dev Tools copilot (/assist-raw) for --prompt; with --run, executes via /raw
  - `--db-assist` — Probe the SQL console copilot: POST /db/assist with this prompt, print raw result
  - `--get` — Generic GET /applications/:appId/<subpath>
  - `--post-path` — Generic POST /applications/:appId/<subpath> (body via --body)
  - `--del` — Generic DELETE /applications/:appId/<subpath>
  - `--abs-get` — Generic GET against an absolute API path (e.g. catalog/installs/:id)
  - `--abs-post` — Generic POST against an absolute API path (e.g. catalog/install-from-yaml), body via --body

### `flui ssh`

SSH into a cluster node

Arguments:
  - `node` (required) — Node to SSH into, as <cluster>/<node> (e.g. my-cluster/master, my-cluster/worker-1). A bare node name (master, worker-1) targets the control cluster.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> master
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> worker-1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> control-cluster/master
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> workload-cluster-1/master
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> workload-cluster-1/worker-1
```

### `flui update`

Update the flui CLI to the latest version

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui version`

Show the CLI version and the platform release it pins (component image tags + bootstrap ref). Useful for debugging an install.

Flags:
  - `--latest` — Show what `env create --latest` would resolve to (mobile tags: bootstrap master, :latest images) instead of the pinned release
  - `--json` — Output as JSON

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --latest
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --json
```

## app

### `flui app alerts`

Show alerts for an application — one row per episode, newest first

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `--firing` — Only alerts still firing
  - `-n, --limit` (default: 20) — How many to show
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --firing
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
```

### `flui app backup create`

Archive an application volume to S3-compatible object storage. When --bucket is omitted the cluster provider auto-provisions one (Scaleway: full-auto using your compute key; Hetzner: requires Object Storage credentials connected). Otherwise pass an explicit endpoint + --bucket and S3 credentials via flags or FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY/FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY env.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-v, --volume` — Volume (PVC) name when the app has multiple volumes. Required if more than one PVC exists.
  - `-d, --description` — Optional human-friendly tag appended to the key prefix
  - `-b, --bucket` — Destination S3 bucket name. Omit to auto-provision via the cluster provider.
  - `-e, --endpoint` — S3 endpoint URL (required when --bucket is set). Examples: https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud, https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
  - `-r, --region` (default: "auto") — S3 region
  - `--access-key` — S3 access key. Defaults to FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY env var.
  - `--secret-key` — S3 secret key. Defaults to FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY env var.
  - `--key-prefix` — Override the destination key prefix (default: flui/<cluster>/<app>/<timestamp>/)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --description nightly
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app -b external-bucket -e https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com -r eu-central-1
```

### `flui app backup delete`

Delete an S3 backup of an application. Removes all objects under the export key prefix.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `exportId` (required) — Export id (S3 key prefix) returned by `flui app backup create`

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-b, --bucket` (required) — S3 bucket where the backup lives
  - `-e, --endpoint` (required) — S3 endpoint URL
  - `-r, --region` (default: "auto") — S3 region
  - `--access-key` — S3 access key id (defaults to FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY env)
  - `--secret-key` — S3 secret access key (defaults to FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY env)
  - `-f, --force` — Skip confirmation

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app flui/<cluster>/<app>/20260510170000-abc123 -b my-bucket -e https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud
```

### `flui app build`

Inspect or refresh the latest build for an application. Use --watch to follow the status until terminal.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text")
  - `--refresh` — Force the backend to re-poll GitHub Actions for the latest build now
  - `-w, --watch` — Poll until the latest build reaches a terminal status (COMPLETED / FAILED / CANCELLED)
  - `--interval` (default: 5) — Polling interval in seconds (with --watch)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --watch
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --refresh
```

### `flui app builds`

List recent builds for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table")
  - `-n, --limit` (default: 10)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --limit 5
```

### `flui app crash`

Show a single crash diagnosis. Use --dismiss to mark it resolved.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `id` (required) — Crash diagnosis ID

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `--dismiss` — Mark this crash diagnosis as resolved
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 5d3f...
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 5d3f... --dismiss
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 5d3f... --output json
```

### `flui app crashes`

Show recent crash diagnoses for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
```

### `flui app delete`

Delete an application and remove all its resources from the cluster. Works for both catalog installs and source-deploy (flui.yaml) apps. System-protected apps require --force.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-f, --force` — Skip confirmation prompt
  - `--no-wait` — Return immediately after queuing the uninstall

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> uptime-kuma
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> uptime-kuma --force
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> uptime-kuma --no-wait
```

### `flui app image delete`

Delete a container image version from the registry (GHCR). Refuses to delete the currently deployed version. The latest-release guard can be overridden with --force.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `versionId` (required) — GitHub Packages numeric version id (from `flui app versions --output json`)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `--force` — Override the latest-release guard. The currently-deployed guard is never bypassable.
  - `-y, --yes` — Skip confirmation prompt

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 845914920
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 845914920 --force
```

### `flui app init`

Copy Flui deploy files (Dockerfile + flui.yaml) from an official framework template into the current directory. Use this on an existing Git repository to make it deployable with `flui deploy`. Run `flui app init --list` to see the supported frameworks and versions.

Arguments:
  - `framework` — Framework template, optionally with a major version pin (e.g. `nextjs` or `nextjs@16`). Omit when using --list.

Flags:
  - `--list` — Print supported frameworks and versions, then exit
  - `--force` — Overwrite existing files without prompting
  - `--dry-run` — Print the actions that would be taken, no file writes
  - `--target` — Target directory (default: current working directory)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nextjs
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nextjs@16
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> fastapi --target ./api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --list
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nestjs --force
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nuxt --dry-run
```

### `flui app list`

List all applications in the cluster

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-x, --expanded` — Show the individual components of composed apps
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --expanded
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui app logs`

Fetch logs for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-l, --level` [error | warn | info | debug] — Filter by log level
  - `-n, --tail` (default: 100) — Number of lines to return
  - `-s, --search` — Full-text search query
  - `--namespace` — Kubernetes namespace (optional, auto-detected from app)
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --level error
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --tail 500
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --search "connection refused"
```

### `flui app manifest`

Print the flui.yaml (kind: Application) schema & annotated example — for humans and LLMs.

Arguments:
  - `framework` — Framework for --example (e.g. nextjs, spring-boot, fastapi). Sets port + healthcheck.

Flags:
  - `--json` — Format output as json.
  - `--example` — Emit a fully-annotated example manifest instead of the field reference.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --json
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --example
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --example nextjs
```

### `flui app metrics`

Show instant Prometheus metrics (CPU/mem/network/replicas) for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
```

### `flui app redeploy`

Redeploy an application from an existing image (tag or digest), without rebuilding

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `target` — Tag, short digest (12+ hex), or full sha256:<digest>

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `--build` — Deploy from an existing build id (alternative to tag/digest)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api a1cac27
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api sha256:812bdfd0a833...
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --build <buildId>
```

### `flui app releases`

List recent releases (deploy/rollback operations) for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table")
  - `--current` — Only show the current (most recent) release
  - `-n, --limit` (default: 10)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --current
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
```

### `flui app restart`

Trigger a rolling restart of an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
```

### `flui app scale`

Scale an application to a desired replica count

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-r, --replicas` (required) — Desired replica count (0 = stop all pods)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --replicas 3
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --replicas 0
```

### `flui app schedule create`

Create a scheduled job (cron) on an application. The job runs the given command on the app's image + env, on the cron schedule. Overlapping runs are skipped by default (concurrency=Forbid).

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-n, --name` (required) — Schedule name (lowercase alphanumeric + dashes)
  - `-s, --schedule` (required) — Cron expression (5 fields), e.g. "0 3 * * *"
  - `-x, --command` (required) — Shell command to run (executed via /bin/sh -c)
  - `-t, --timezone` — IANA timezone (e.g. Europe/Rome). Default: cluster time
  - `--concurrency` [Allow | Forbid | Replace] (default: "Forbid") — Overlap policy
  - `--disabled` — Create the schedule suspended (not running)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --name nightly-cleanup --schedule "0 3 * * *" --command "node dist/cleanup.js"
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app -n report -s "*/15 * * * *" -x "php artisan report:run" --timezone Europe/Rome
```

### `flui app schedule delete`

Delete a scheduled job (cron) from an application.

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `name` (required) — Schedule name

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app schedule list`

List the scheduled jobs (cron) of an application. Each runs a command on the app's image + env on a cron schedule.

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --output json
```

### `flui app schedule logs`

Show the logs of a scheduled-job run. Defaults to the most recent run; use --run to target a specific one (see `flui app schedule runs`).

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `name` (required) — Schedule name

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-r, --run` — Specific run (Job) name. Default: most recent run

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app nightly-cleanup
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app nightly-cleanup --run my-app-nightly-cleanup-28912345
```

### `flui app schedule runs`

List the recent runs of a scheduled job with their status. History depth follows the CronJob retention limits.

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `name` (required) — Schedule name

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app schedule trigger`

Trigger a scheduled job now, independently of its cron timing. Creates a one-off run from the schedule.

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `name` (required) — Schedule name

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app snapshot create`

Create a snapshot of an application volume. Today on every provider this is a full PVC clone built via the copy-pod export primitive (sink=pvc-clone) because workload PVCs use local-path. Cost: a full Volume per snapshot.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-v, --volume` — Volume (PVC) name when the app has multiple volumes. Required if more than one PVC exists.
  - `-d, --description` — Optional human-friendly tag appended to the snapshot id

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --description before-upgrade
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --volume data
```

### `flui app snapshot delete`

Delete a volume snapshot of an application.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `snapshotId` (required) — Snapshot id (from `flui app snapshot list`)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-f, --force` — Skip confirmation

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app my-app-snap-20260510-abcdef
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app my-app-snap-... --force
```

### `flui app snapshot list`

List volume snapshots. Use --app to filter to a single app, omit to list cluster-wide.

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-a, --app` — Filter by application name or slug
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --app my-app
```

### `flui app snapshot restore`

Restore a snapshot into a new side-by-side PVC. The application is not touched — the new PVC is created in the same namespace and can be promoted later with `flui app snapshot swap`.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `snapshotId` (required) — Snapshot id (from `flui app snapshot list`)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)

### `flui env create`

Create control cluster infrastructure on K3s

Flags:
  - `-p, --provider` [hetzner | scaleway] — Cloud provider for the control cluster (default: the profile's configured provider)
  - `--node-size` — Server type for cluster nodes (run "flui server-types list --provider <provider>" to see available types). Defaults to the provider recommended size.
  - `-r, --region` — Region/location code. Defaults to the provider default region.
  - `--node-count` (default: 0) — Number of worker nodes (0 = master-only, default: 0)
  - `--disk-size` — Root disk size in GB. Required for network-storage instance types (Scaleway PRO2, ENT1). Optional for local-SSD types — defaults to the included size of the instance type.
  - `-d, --detached` — Detached mode: start cluster creation and exit immediately
  - `--wait` — Wait for cluster to be ready before returning (polls operation status)
  - `--configure-firewall` — Automatically configure firewall after cluster creation
  - `--firewall-ip` — Source IP/CIDR for firewall (comma-separated, default: auto-detect)
  - `--auth-mode` (default: "oidc") — Authentication mode (only oidc is supported)
  - `--acme-staging` — Use Let's Encrypt staging endpoint (untrusted cert, no rate limits) — useful while iterating to avoid burning prod quota
  - `--latest` — Install mobile dev tags instead of the pinned release: bootstrap scripts from `master` and `:latest` Docker images. Default: every component is pinned to the CLI release version.
  - `--no-shared-storage` — Disable Flui shared storage (NFS+fscache). Default: shared storage enabled — master gets a Volume hosting the NFS export, workers mount it. Disable to fall back to local-path on each node bundled disk.
  - `--shared-storage-size` (default: 20) — Size in GB of the master shared storage Volume (only when shared storage is enabled). Default: 20.
  - `--host` — BYOS: install onto an existing Linux host (IP or DNS) over SSH instead of provisioning via a cloud provider. Enables BYOS mode.
  - `--port` (default: 22) — BYOS: SSH port of --host (default: 22)
  - `--user` (default: "root") — BYOS: SSH user for --host (default: root)
  - `--ssh-key` — BYOS: SSH private key for --host. Optional — if omitted, Flui reuses an existing key that already works, otherwise it authorizes one (asking for the host password once) and never stores the password. A passphrase-protected key is supported only when loaded in your ssh-agent (run `ssh-add` first).
  - `--ssh-password` — BYOS: host password, for non-interactive key authorization (e.g. CI). Prefer the FLUI_SSH_PASSWORD env var to keep it out of shell history. Used only in-memory to install the key, then auth switches to the key.
  - `--master-public-ip` — BYOS: externally reachable IP of --host (defaults to --host); used for endpoints/TLS
  - `--skip-precheck` — BYOS: skip the host readiness precheck
  - `--best-effort` — BYOS: continue even if the precheck reports problems
  - `--local-stub` — BYOS (dev): stop after bootstrap + CA check; skip observability/kubeconfig/secret patch. Use with BOOTSTRAP_SCRIPTS_URL=file://… for local Podman testing.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --node-size cx32
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -d
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --region fsn1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --wait
```

  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --output json
```

## iam

### `flui iam apply`

Apply an AccessPolicy file (idempotent upsert of grants; --prune for full sync).

Flags:
  - `-f, --file` (required) — Path to the AccessPolicy YAML/JSON file
  - `--prune` — Delete existing grants not present in the file (full sync). Off by default.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -f access-policy.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -f access-policy.yaml --prune
```

### `flui iam export`

Export all access grants as a kind: AccessPolicy document (config-as-code snapshot). YAML by default.

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [yaml | json] (default: "yaml") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> > access-policy.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui iam grant add`

Create an access grant: bind a principal to a role at a scope. Scope is one of everything (global), a cluster, a portal section, or a selector over app attributes (kind/project/provider/tags/slugs — AND-ed; tags match ALL).

Flags:
  - `-t, --type` [user | group | service_account] (default: "user") — Principal type
  - `-p, --principal` (required) — Principal reference (email, group name, or service-account id)
  - `-r, --role` [viewer | editor | manager] (required) — Role to grant
  - `-s, --scope` [global | cluster | section | selector] (default: "global") — Scope type
  - `--cluster` — Cluster id (scope=cluster)
  - `--section` — Portal section key (scope=section)
  - `--kind` — App kind, e.g. DATABASE (scope=selector)
  - `--project` — Project (scope=selector)
  - `--provider` — Provider (scope=selector)
  - `--cluster-id` — Cluster id (scope=selector)
  - `--cluster-name` — Cluster name (scope=selector)
  - `--app-type` [system | user] — App type (scope=selector)
  - `--app` — App slug — repeatable (scope=selector)
  - `--tag` — Tag — repeatable, app must carry ALL (scope=selector)
  - `--selector` — Raw selector JSON (overrides individual selector flags)
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p alice@acme.com -r manager
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -t group -p platform -r viewer -s cluster --cluster c1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p bob@acme.com -r editor -s selector --kind DATABASE
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p ci-deployer -t service_account -r editor -s selector --app acme-api --app acme-web
```

### `flui iam grant list`

List access grants (role bindings).

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui iam grant remove`

Remove an access grant by id.

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Grant id (from `flui iam grant list`)

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes` — Skip the confirmation prompt

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> 3f9a…
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> 3f9a… --yes
```

### `flui iam group add-member`

Add a member (by email) to a Flui-local group.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Group name
  - `email` (required) — Member email

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> platform alice@acme.com
```

### `flui iam group create`

Create a Flui-local group. Name is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Group name

Flags:
  - `-d, --description` — Group description
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> platform
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme-team --description "Acme team"
```

### `flui iam group delete`

Delete a Flui-local group. Grants targeting this group stop matching.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Group name

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes` — Skip the confirmation prompt

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme-team
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme-team --yes
```

### `flui iam group list`

List Flui-local groups (membership lives in Flui, not the IdP).

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui iam group remove-member`

Remove a member (by email) from a Flui-local group.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Group name
  - `email` (required) — Member email

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> platform alice@acme.com
```

### `flui iam roles`

List the built-in access roles and the permissions each one grants.

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui iam whoami`

Show the effective permissions of the currently authenticated identity.

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

## integration

### `flui integration connect`

Connect a third-party integration to your Flui account. Currently supports GitHub: opens a browser to install the Flui GitHub App, then waits for the local callback to confirm the connection.

Arguments:
  - `provider` (required) — Integration provider (currently only `github`)

Flags:
  - `--headless` — Print the install URL instead of opening a browser (useful over SSH)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github --headless
```

### `flui integration ghcr-pat revoke`

Revoke the GHCR PAT stored in Flui. Does NOT revoke the token on GitHub — do that separately at https://github.com/settings/tokens. After revoking, `flui deploy` will fail until a new PAT is set.

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes` — Skip the confirmation prompt

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --yes
```

### `flui integration ghcr-pat set`

Save (or replace) the GitHub classic PAT used by Flui to pull container images from GHCR. Required for `flui deploy` to work — GitHub App and OAuth tokens cannot read container packages (see https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/34084).

Flags:
  - `--headless` — Print the GitHub token-creation URL instead of opening a browser (useful over SSH)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --headless
```

### `flui integration ghcr-pat status`

Show the current state of the GHCR PAT used by Flui to pull container images from GHCR.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui integration installations`

List all GitHub App installations tracked by Flui. Requires admin privileges. Use the `installationId` shown here with `flui integration remove-installation` to delete a stale or wrong record.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui integration list`

List third-party integrations configured for your account and show whether each is connected.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui integration remove-installation`

Remove a GitHub App installation record from the Flui database. Requires admin privileges. Does NOT uninstall the app on GitHub — uninstall it there first, otherwise the next webhook will re-create the record.

Arguments:
  - `installationId` (required) — GitHub installation ID (numeric). Get it with `flui integration installations`.

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes` — Skip the confirmation prompt

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> 12345678
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> 12345678 --yes
```

### `flui integration reset`

Remove the instance-wide GitHub integration (admin). Clears the stored config plus all per-user tokens and App installations. Users will need to reconnect afterwards.

Arguments:
  - `provider` (required) — Integration provider (currently only `github`)

Flags:
  - `--yes` — Skip the typed confirmation (for scripts / CI)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github --yes
```

### `flui integration setup`

Guided GitHub integration setup (admin). Pick GitHub App (recommended, creates the App on GitHub via manifest flow) or Personal Access Token (validates and saves a token).

Arguments:
  - `provider` (required) — Integration provider (currently only `github`)

Flags:
  - `--headless` — Print URLs instead of opening a browser

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github --headless
```

### `flui integration setup-github-app`

Configure the GitHub App credentials in Flui (admin only). Interactively prompts for App ID, slug, client ID/secret, webhook secret and private key path. Secrets are hidden during input and encrypted at rest in the database.

Flags:
  - `--private-key-file` — Path to the GitHub App private key PEM file (skips the path prompt)
  - `--callback-url` — OAuth callback URL configured on the GitHub App. Defaults to <api-url>/repositories/github-app/user-callback

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --private-key-file ./flui-cloud.pem
```

### `flui integration status`

Show the current GitHub integration status: configured mode, live health check, and (in PAT mode) your own connection state.

Arguments:
  - `provider` (required) — Integration provider (currently only `github`)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github
```

## migrate

### `flui migrate app abort`

Abort an app migration before cutover (destination torn down, source untouched)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate app create`

Move an application workload to another cluster

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application to move (name or id)

Flags:
  - `-t, --to` (required) — Target cluster name or id
  - `-f, --from` — Source cluster name or id (default: auto-detect)
  - `--cutover` [auto | manual] (default: "auto") — Cutover mode

### `flui migrate app cutover`

Fire the cutover for a parked (manual) app migration

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

### `flui migrate app destroy-source`

Destroy the drained source workload after cutover (irreversible)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate app list`

List app-workload migrations

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate app show`

Show an app-workload migration by id

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate db abort`

Abort a DB migration before cutover (replication link + destination torn down, source untouched)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate db create`

Move a managed-Postgres app to another cluster

Arguments:
  - `dbapp` (required) — Managed-Postgres app to move

Flags:
  - `-t, --to` (required) — Target cluster name or id
  - `-f, --from` — Source cluster name or id (default: auto-detect)
  - `--mode` [live | restore] (default: "live") — Migration mode
  - `--cutover` [auto | manual] (default: "auto") — Cutover mode
  - `--at` — restore mode only: ISO-8601 instant to recover to
  - `--name` — display name for the new install
  - `--verify` — exact per-table count(*) comparison at cutover

### `flui migrate db cutover`

Fire the cutover for a parked (manual) DB migration

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

### `flui migrate db list`

List managed-Postgres migrations

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate db show`

Show a managed-Postgres migration by id

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate full abort`

Abort a full migration before cutover (both legs torn down, source untouched)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate full create`

Move a consumer app together with its managed-Postgres data

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Consumer application to move

Flags:
  - `--db` (required) — Managed-Postgres app (name or id) whose data migrates with the app
  - `-t, --to` (required) — Target cluster name or id
  - `-f, --from` — Source cluster name or id (default: auto-detect)
  - `--cutover` [auto | manual] (default: "auto") — Cutover mode
  - `--staging` [scaled-down | live-fenced] (default: "scaled-down") — Staging mode for the destination app before cutover

### `flui migrate full cutover`

Fire the cutover for a parked (manual) full migration

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

### `flui migrate full destroy-source`

Destroy the drained source app workload after cutover (irreversible)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate full list`

List full-app migrations

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate full show`

Show a full-app migration by id

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `--json`

## node

### `flui node add`

Add worker node(s) to the cluster. Provisions new servers and joins them to K3s.

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-n, --count` (default: 1) — Number of workers to add (1-5)
  - `--no-wait` — Return immediately after queuing the operation

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --count 2
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --count 3 --no-wait
```

### `flui node connect`

BYOS: join an existing Linux host to the cluster as a worker node (over SSH, no provisioning).

Flags:
  - `--host` (required) — IP or DNS of the existing host to join as a worker
  - `--port` (default: 22) — SSH port of --host
  - `--user` (default: "root") — SSH user for --host
  - `--ssh-key` — Path to the SSH private key that already authenticates to --host (default: ~/.ssh/id_rsa)
  - `--master-ip` — Address the new node uses to reach the master k3s API (https://<addr>:6443). Defaults to the cluster master IP.
  - `--node-network` — CIDR of the private network the nodes share (host firewall must allow it for node-to-node k3s traffic). Defaults to the /24 of the detected private IP.
  - `--skip-precheck` — Skip the host readiness precheck
  - `--best-effort` — Continue even if the precheck reports problems

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --host 203.0.113.10
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --host 10.0.0.12 --master-ip 10.0.0.11 --node-network 10.0.0.0/24
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --host localhost --port 2223 --ssh-key ~/.flui/byos-local/operator_key --master-ip 10.89.0.2
```

### `flui node list`

List all nodes in the cluster (master + workers)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui node remove`

Cordon, drain and remove a worker node from the cluster. Cannot remove the master.

Arguments:
  - `nodeId` (required) — Node ID to remove (from `flui node list`)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `--no-wait` — Return immediately after queuing the operation

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> <node-id>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> <node-id> --no-wait
```

## repo

### `flui repo connect`

Connect (import) a GitHub repository into your Flui account so it can be deployed with `flui deploy`. Pass the full name `owner/repo`, or omit it for an interactive picker over the repositories accessible via your GitHub integration.

Arguments:
  - `repo` — Full repository name `owner/repo`. Omit to pick interactively.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme/my-app
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui repo disconnect`

Disconnect a repository from your Flui account. Requires admin privileges. Does not delete the repository on GitHub.

Arguments:
  - `repo` (required) — Full repository name `owner/repo`

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes` — Skip the confirmation prompt

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme/my-app
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme/my-app --yes
```

### `flui repo list`

List repositories connected to your Flui account.

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

## server-types

### `flui server-types list`

List available server types for a provider

Flags:
  - `-p, --provider` [hetzner | scaleway] (required) — Cloud provider
  - `-r, --region` — Filter by region/location
  - `-m, --memory` — Filter by RAM in GB: exact "16", range "8-32", min "8-", or max "-32"
  - `-s, --sort` [price | memory | cores | disk | name] (default: "price") — Sort by field
  - `--desc` — Sort in descending order
  - `--json` — Output as JSON
  - `--force-refresh` — Force refresh cache from API

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --region fsn1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory 16
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory 8-32
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory -32
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --sort memory
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --sort price --desc
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --json
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --force-refresh
```

## template

### `flui template use`

Create a new GitHub repository from a Flui framework template and connect it to your account.

Arguments:
  - `framework` (required) — Framework template to use (e.g. astro, nextjs, nestjs)
  - `name` (required) — Name for the new GitHub repository

Flags:
  - `--org` — GitHub organisation or user to create the repo under (default: your account)
  - `-d, --description` — Repository description
  - `--public` — Create as a public repository (default: private)
  - `--no-import` — Skip auto-importing the repository into Flui

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> astro my-astro-site
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nextjs my-app --public
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nestjs my-api --org my-org
```

sections.title: Applications
sections.body:
The `app` topic groups every command that acts on an application
running in a cluster — both catalog installs (`kind: CatalogApp`) and
source-built apps (`kind: Application`). The behavior is identical on
both sides: the application is the unit of operation, regardless of
how its image got into the registry.

Almost every verb under `app` takes an application name or slug as its
first positional argument, and accepts `-c, --cluster <name|id>` to pick
the cluster (auto-detected when the active profile has only one). The few
output flags follow the same pattern as the rest of the CLI: `-o,
--output table|json` (or `text|json` on the streaming commands), `-f,
--force` to skip confirmations, `--no-wait` to queue and exit. The one
exception is `flui app init`, which runs locally to scaffold a new
project before any application exists — see [Project setup](#project-setup).

The sections below group the commands by intent: project setup,
inspection, runtime diagnostics, release management, lifecycle, data
management, and deletion.

## Project setup

### `flui app init [<framework>]`

Copies Flui's deploy files — a `Dockerfile` and a `flui.yaml` — from an
official framework template into the current directory, turning an
existing Git repository into something `flui deploy` can build. Unlike
every other `app` verb it runs locally and does not target a running
application.

```bash
flui app init --list           # list supported frameworks and versions
flui app init nextjs           # scaffold for the latest supported Next.js
flui app init nextjs@16        # pin a major version
flui app init fastapi --target ./api
flui app init nestjs --force   # overwrite existing files
flui app init nuxt --dry-run   # print the actions, write nothing
```

| Flag / Arg | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<framework>` | Framework template, optionally with a major-version pin (`nextjs`, `nextjs@16`). Omit when using `--list`. |
| `--list` | Print the supported frameworks and versions, then exit. |
| `--force` | Overwrite existing files without prompting. |
| `--dry-run` | Print the actions that would be taken; write nothing. |
| `--target <dir>` | Target directory. Default: the current working directory. |

`app init` adds Flui files to a repository you already have. To create a
*new* repository from a template instead, use `flui template use` — see
[Templates](/cli/templates/).

## Inspection

### `flui app list`

Lists the applications in the cluster with their high-level state.

```bash
flui app list
flui app list --output json
```

### `flui app status <name>`

Shows the live runtime status of one application: how many replicas
are ready vs desired, the current release, and any condition that
needs attention.

```bash
flui app status my-api
flui app status my-api --output json
```

### `flui app logs <name>`

Streams application logs from the cluster. By default returns the
last 100 lines; filter by level, full-text search, or bump the
window.

```bash
flui app logs my-api
flui app logs my-api --level error
flui app logs my-api --tail 500
flui app logs my-api --search "connection refused"
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-l, --level` | — | Filter by `error`, `warn`, `info`, `debug`. |
| `-n, --tail <n>` | `100` | Number of lines to return. |
| `-s, --search <q>` | — | Full-text search. |
| `--namespace <ns>` | auto-detected | Override the namespace; rarely needed. |
| `-o, --output text\|json` | `text` | Output format. |

### `flui app metrics <name>`

Instant resource metrics for one application: CPU, memory, network
I/O, replica count. Useful to spot-check a workload's footprint or
correlate a spike with a deploy.

```bash
flui app metrics my-api
flui app metrics my-api --output json
```

## Runtime diagnostics

### `flui app crashes <name>`

Lists recent **crash diagnoses** for the application — automatic
reports produced when a workload restarted unexpectedly, summarising
the exit code, the signals the runtime saw, and the probable cause.

```bash
flui app crashes my-api
flui app crashes my-api --output json
```

### `flui app crash <name> <id>`

Shows one crash diagnosis in full, including the full reasoning chain
